"Minnie the Moocher" was written by the famous band leader, jazz composer and singer Cabell "Cab" Calloway III, and the jazz music publisher Irving Mills. It was first recorded in 1931 by Cab Calloway and His Orchestra, and became their signature song for the next decade. The song is based lyrically on Frankie "Half-Pint" Jaxon's 1927 "Willie the Weeper"

The song tells the sad story of a "red hot hoochie coocher" girl called Minnie. The hoochie coochie was a style of belly dancing with non-respectable gypsy origins, and was considered lecherous at the time. The licentious Minnie gets involved with a "kokie" conveniently called Smokey, a "kokie" being someone who takes cocaine. Kokie takes her down to Chinatown where he introduces her to opium, which is what Calloway meant when using the jive expression "to kick the gong around" in the lyrics. The rest of the song describes her opium-induced wish-fulfillment fantasy in which the king of Sweden gives her many gifts, including "a diamond car, with the puh-latinum wheels." Calloway doesn't tell us how this story ends, but he does wail "Poor Min! Poor Min" Poo-oor Min" at the end, which may be an indication that Minnie's a goner.

The November 22, 1951 issue of Jet magazine gives this account of the "Minnie" on whom the song was based: "Minnie "The Moocher" has died. She was a familiar figure In downtown Indianapolis. A 82-year-old woman whose real name was Minnie Gayton, she acquired the quaint nickname of "The Moocher" by regularly begging food from grocers and carting it off in a baby buggy. She slept in doorways, on porches and in garages. During the record-breaking blizzard, her body was found on a porch, blanketed with snow. She died from exposure."
I always thought "cokie" was an allusion to coke as in coal, meaning he was black.
Remember, this was the 20's and 30's. It may have evolved to mean black, dunno. Also, muggles weren't new to Harry Potter, it originally was a term for a marijuana cigarette.

"Coke" had already been in use for centuries to refer to coal, a common fuel and common reference to anything dark, similar to "tar" and "pitch." So I have to imagine that audiences of the time would think of that first. Using it to describe complexion also carries symmetry with the "hoochie coochie," which hints at her own social status. Then the "King of Sweden" evokes an image totally contrasting with a complexion of coal, reinforcing the idea that she originally loved Smokey despite his low-status look.

If that's all true, then the drug story introduces a deniable dual meaning. The word referred to cocaine and Coca Cola, apparently for a couple of decades by the 1930s. So both meanings of "cokie" at the same time make sense, and it adds an interesting depth to the story.

And if "poor Min" were really "poor men," like it sounds, that fits with how Smokey feels after playing around with a fickle moocher. But it works for both, pulling both stories together, lamenting all parties involved. Maybe I'm overthinking it, but it makes sense to me this way.

Good job. You have presented as good an analysis as the source I quoted, in fact better.

As for the "King of Sweden", I also saw this discussed in reference to the Willie The Weeper song mentioned (an influence of this song):

"Willie the Weeper" is also about drug addiction and an ensuing dream, but instead of the king of Sweden, Willie dreams of his adventures with the Queen of Sheba, Cleopatra, and the sultan of Turkey.

So a case could be made Cab was thinking of this when he sang about the King.

Also, Cab continued with other songs featuring Minnie:

Calloway also wrote an extended version, adding verses that describe Minnie and Smokey going to jail; Minnie pays Smokey's bail, but he abandons her there. Another verse describes her tempting "Deacon Lowdown" when she "wiggled her jelly roll at him". Finally, they took Minnie to "where they put the crazies", where she dies. This explains why both the short version and the long version end with the words "Poor Min, poor Min".

"Minnie the Moocher's Wedding Day", "Ghost of Smoky Joe", "Kickin' the Gong Around", "Minnie's a Hepcat Now", "Mister Paganini - Swing for Minnie", "We Go Well Together", and "Zah Zuh Zaz". Some of these songs indicate that Minnie's boyfriend Smoky was named Smoky Joe as well.
